*   **Limitations:** Low precision compared to explicit methods; suffers from spikes and rotational artifacts; requires high resolution for acceptable accuracy [S1, unofficial].

The claim lists three specific limitations of the texture-based approach described in Source [S1]: 1) Low precision compared to explicit methods (supported by the text: 'a texture-based approach will never get close to the precision of an explicit calculation'); 2) Suffers from spikes and rotational artifacts (supported by the text: 'unpleasant spikes across the viewport' and 'produce rotational artifacts'); 3) Requires high resolution for acceptable accuracy (supported by the text: 'can be limited by increasing texture resolution' and 'highly dependable on the resolution'). All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
*   **Strengths:** Demonstrates precision limits and rotational artifacts of texture-based approximations [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the evidence demonstrates precision limits and rotational artifacts of texture-based approximations. Source [S1] explicitly states that 'a texture-based approach will never get close to the precision of an explicit calculation without considerably increasing the number of grid cells' (supporting precision limits) and that 'the texture-based approach (i.e., red graph) produces unstable and faulty results throughout the entire rotation... it is a common observation that many texture-based approaches produce rotational artifacts' (supporting rotational artifacts).

Each cell $c_i$ has a defined area $\text{area}(c_i)$ [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly defines the grid $G$ as consisting of cells $c_i$. In the formula for the density of a cell (Equation 2.3), the term $area(c_i)$ appears in the denominator. For this mathematical operation to be valid and defined, the area of each cell $c_i$ must be a defined quantity. Therefore, the evidence supports the claim that each cell has a defined area.

The claim states that there is a list of $N_t$ triangles $t_k$. This confirms the existence of a list or set of $N_t$ triangles indexed by $k$.

*   **Rotational Artifacts:** The texture-based approach produces unstable and faulty results during rotation, unlike explicit calculations which remain smooth [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the texture-based approach produces unstable and faulty results during rotation, unlike explicit calculations which remain smooth. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'It is evident that the texture-based approach (i.e., red graph) produces unstable and faulty results throughout the entire rotation, while an explicit calculation allows smooth transitions at all times.' This directly supports every fact in the claim.

*   **When to use:** As a diagnostic tool to evaluate texture-based volume rendering suitability [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the evidence supports the use of the described method as a diagnostic tool to evaluate texture-based volume rendering suitability. Source [S1] explicitly states in the introduction to Section 2.3.1 that the 2D test application (Sm2D) was implemented 'In order to investigate the applicability of a texture-based approach for smoke volumes.' Furthermore, Section 2.3.2 concludes by stating that comparing the results 'allows one to conclude whether this approach might be suitable for smoke volume rendering.' The evidence details the implementation and results of this specific diagnostic experiment.
supported
*   **When not to use:** When high precision or smooth rotational transitions are required [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the texture-based approach produces 'unstable and faulty results' and 'rotational artifacts' compared to explicit calculations which allow 'smooth transitions'. It also notes that the approach lacks precision without significantly increasing grid cells. Therefore, the claim that it should not be used when high precision or smooth rotational transitions are required is fully supported by the text.

The evidence explicitly states that the viewport simplifies to a 1-dimensional function (Section 2.3.1, Experiment) and that the results alpha(r_j) are visualized in an output box interpreted as the viewport edge with accumulated values on the Y-axis (Section 2.3.1, Output). This confirms that the absorption coefficient is visualized as a one-dimensional function across the viewport edge.

It sets itself apart from its siblings by serving as a diagnostic tool to demonstrate the precision limits and rotational artifacts inherent in texture-based approximations compared to explicit geometric calculations [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the test application (Sm2D) was implemented to 'investigate the applicability of a texture-based approach' and compares it against an 'explicit calculation'. It confirms that the texture-based approach suffers from 'unpleasant spikes' (artifacts) and 'unstable and faulty results' during rotation (rotational artifacts), and that it cannot match the precision of explicit calculations without significantly increasing grid resolution. This aligns perfectly with the claim that the tool demonstrates precision limits and rotational artifacts inherent in texture-based approximations compared to explicit geometric calculations.
